claim: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae Lge1 protein is required for histone H2B ubiquitination.
source: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae Lge1 protein is required for histone H2B ubiquitination and its N-terminal intrinsically disordered fragment (Lge11-80) undergoes robust phase separation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about Lge1 protein function.

claim: The N-terminal intrinsically disordered fragment Lge11-80 undergoes robust phase separation.
source: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae Lge1 protein is required for histone H2B ubiquitination and its N-terminal intrinsically disordered fragment (Lge11-80) undergoes robust phase separation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Lge11-80 is enriched in Y, R, and G residues.
source: Lge11-80 exhibits a strong compositional bias shared by many known phase-separating proteins (enriched in Y, R, and G, Figure 1A)
evidence: The sequence composition is shown in Figure 1A and stated in the text.

claim: Lge11-80 is fully disordered.
source: Lge11-80 exhibits a strong compositional bias shared by many known phase-separating proteins (enriched in Y, R, and G, Figure 1A), is fully disordered, and undergoes phase separation readily (Gallego et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and referenced to prior work.

claim: WT Lge11-80 phase separates at a protein concentration of 1 µM in 0.1 M NaCl.
source: WT Lge11-80 phase separates already at a protein concentration of 1 µM in 0.1 M NaCl (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: WT Lge11-80 phase separation can be inhibited at high salt concentration (>2 M NaCl).
source: Its phase separation is robust and can be inhibited at high salt concentration (>2 M NaCl).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the solubility diagrams.

claim: Mutating all arginine residues in WT Lge11-80 to lysine (R>K mutant) increases the csat for phase separation by approximately 10-fold.
source: Mutating all arginine residues in WT Lge11-80 to lysine (R>K mutant) increases the csat for phase separation by approximately 10-fold under the conditions tested (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The Y>A substitution strongly impairs phase separation.
source: At the same time, Y>A mutations strongly impair phase separation (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, see also Gallego et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in figures, with reference to prior work.

claim: Tyrosines play a critical role in WT and R>K phase separation.
source: At the same time, Y>A mutations strongly impair phase separation (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, see also Gallego et al., 2020), suggesting that tyrosines play a critical role in WT and R>K phase separation (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that Y>A mutation impairs phase separation.

claim: π-π interactions are important in biomolecular condensate formation.
source: suggesting that tyrosines play a critical role in WT and R>K phase separation (Figure 1C) and highlighting the importance of π-π interactions in biomolecular condensate formation, as proposed earlier (Vernon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the role of tyrosines and referenced to prior work.

claim: At protein concentration of 45 μM and above, the Y>A mutant results in sporadic amorphous precipitates.
source: Finally, we note that at protein concentration of 45 μM and above, the Y>A mutant results in sporadic amorphous precipitates (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The WT and R>K recovery half-times are in the range of 100 s for partial bleaching.
source: Thus, the WT and R>K recovery half-times are in the range of 100 s for partial bleaching, and increase up to 350 s for bleaching of the whole condensates under the conditions tested.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on FRAP experiments.

claim: The recovery half-time for the whole bleached WT condensates is approximately 30% higher than for R>K.
source: Importantly, the recovery half-time for the whole bleached WT condensates is approximately 30% higher than for R>K (Figure 1E), suggesting a potentially different internal organization of the two types of condensates.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ΔG(Y-Y) is independent of the polarity of the environment (approx. –5 kcal/mol on average).
source: Interestingly, ΔG(Y-Y) is independent of the polarity of the environment (approx. –5 kcal/mol on average), while ΔG(R-Y) and ΔG(K-Y) depend significantly on the dielectric permittivity of the medium (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is stated based on Monte Carlo simulation results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ΔG(R-Y) and ΔG(K-Y) depend significantly on the dielectric permittivity of the medium.
source: Interestingly, ΔG(Y-Y) is independent of the polarity of the environment (approx. –5 kcal/mol on average), while ΔG(R-Y) and ΔG(K-Y) depend significantly on the dielectric permittivity of the medium (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is stated based on Monte Carlo simulation results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Both ΔG(R-Y) and ΔG(K-Y) are lowest in the apolar environment (approx. –10 kcal/mol on average).
source: Overall, both ΔG(R-Y) and ΔG(K-Y) are lowest in the apolar environment (approx. –10 kcal/mol on average), intermediate in bulk water (approx. –7.5 kcal/mol on average), and highest at intermediate polarity, where they are comparable to ΔG(Y-Y).
evidence: This is stated based on Monte Carlo simulation results.

claim: Significantly stronger R-Y binding as compared to K-Y was observed only in the environments of intermediate polarity.
source: In our simulations, significantly stronger R-Y binding as compared to K-Y was observed only in the environments of intermediate polarity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated based on Monte Carlo simulation results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The WT 24-copy system forms a single percolating cluster over the last 0.3 µs with all copies of the protein engaged.
source: Specifically, the WT 24-copy system forms a single percolating cluster over the last 0.3 µs (Figure 2C) with all copies of the protein engaged.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C based on MD simulations.

claim: The mutants do not form an extensive interaction network, but rather associate in multiple, differently sized clusters.
source: On the other hand, the mutants do not form such an extensive interaction network, but rather associate in multiple, differently sized clusters.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MD simulations.

claim: R-Y contacts dominate in WT (10% of all possible pairs).
source: The large continuous WT cluster is shaped by π-π interactions (Figure 2A and B) between the most abundant amino acids (R, Y, G), whereby R-Y contacts dominate (10% of all possible pairs, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A based on MD simulations.

claim: G-Y and Y-Y contacts follow R-Y contacts closely (7% of all possible pairs each).
source: The large continuous WT cluster is shaped by π-π interactions (Figure 2A and B) between the most abundant amino acids (R, Y, G), whereby R-Y contacts dominate (10% of all possible pairs, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), followed closely by G-Y and Y-Y contacts (7% of all possible pairs each, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B based on MD simulations.

claim: Both R-Y and Y-Y contacts are strongly enriched over the sequence background, especially in the intermolecular context.
source: In particular, both R-Y and Y-Y contacts are strongly enriched over the sequence background (see Methods for definition), especially in the intermolecular context, that is between different protein chains in multi-chain WT simulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B based on MD simulations.

claim: R>K substitutions increase the importance of G-Y contacts with respect to multi-chain interactions.
source: Interestingly, R>K substitutions increase the importance of G-Y contacts with respect to multi-chain interactions, where they rank top and are even more enriched than K-Y contacts.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MD simulations.

claim: For both WT and R>K Lge11-80 variants the Y-Y contacts are enriched with respect to intramolecular interactions in single-chain simulations and become even more enriched in intermolecular interactions in multi-chain ones.
source: At the same time, for both WT and R>K Lge11-80 variants the Y-Y contacts are enriched with respect to intramolecular interactions in single-chain simulations and become even more enriched in intermolecular interactions in multi-chain ones (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A based on MD simulations.

claim: R-Y is the top contact type in WT and together with Y-Y drives the multi-chain association of this IDR.
source: Altogether, our results show that R-Y is the top contact type in WT and together with Y-Y drives the multi-chain association of this IDR, in agreement with recent observations (Bremer et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MD simulations and referenced to prior work.

claim: Interaction valency stabilizes in the course of WT simulations and reaches the average value of approximately 4 over the last 0.3 µs.
source: Interaction valency, defined as the average number of binding partners per protein molecule, stabilizes in the course of WT simulations and reaches the average value of approximately 4 over the last 0.3 µs (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D based on MD simulations.

claim: Individual WT copies have anywhere between 1 and 9 partners at some point.
source: Interaction valency, defined as the average number of binding partners per protein molecule, stabilizes in the course of WT simulations and reaches the average value of approximately 4 over the last 0.3 µs (Figure 2D), with individual WT copies having anywhere between 1 and 9 partners at some point (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2E based on MD simulations.

claim: Multiple non-interacting protein copies are observed for the two mutants throughout the simulations, with the average valencies plateauing around 2.
source: In contrast, multiple non-interacting protein copies are still observed for the two mutants throughout the simulations, with the average valencies plateauing around 2 and the maximum number of partners not exceeding 6 in either case (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2E based on MD simulations.

claim: Mutations with impaired phase separation exhibit a significantly lower valency of protein-protein interactions in simulations.
source: Thus, mutations with impaired phase separation as detected experimentally exhibit a significantly lower valency of protein-protein interactions in our simulations (see Supplementary file 1 for details).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MD simulations.

claim: The WT contact probability reaches a level that is ~1.5-fold higher than for either mutant.
source: Notably, the WT contact probability reaches a level that is ~1.5-fold higher than for either mutant.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MD simulations.

claim: The WT contact probability is sufficient to form a single percolating cluster with all 24 copies interconnected.
source: This contact probability is sufficient to form a single percolating cluster with all 24 copies interconnected, and is thus higher than the critical contact probability at which one expects the network transition, which is not seen for the two Lge11-80 mutants (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C based on MD simulations.

claim: The interactions between IDPs in simulations are characterized by a dynamic binding mode where the interacting sequence motifs ('stickers') and the non-interacting sequence motifs ('spacers') can be described only statistically.
source: The interactions between IDPs in our simulations are characterized by a dynamic binding mode where the interacting sequence motifs ('stickers') and the non-interacting sequence motifs ('spacers') (Martin et al., 2020) can be described only statistically, and no well-defined, specific structural organization of protein complexes is detected (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A based on MD simulations.

claim: For WT, the typical binding mode is characterized by different partners binding along the sequence in multiple, highly interactive regions.
source: For WT, the typical binding mode, which corresponds to the average valency of 4, is characterized by different partners binding along the sequence in multiple, highly interactive regions (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A and B based on MD simulations.

claim: Both mutants display fewer prominent interaction motifs.
source: In line with valency decrease, both mutants display fewer prominent interaction motifs, whereby for the phase separation-disruptive Y>A mutant intermolecular binding is detected for the C-terminal third of the molecule only (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A based on MD simulations.

claim: For the Y>A mutant intermolecular binding is detected for the C-terminal third of the molecule only.
source: In line with valency decrease, both mutants display fewer prominent interaction motifs, whereby for the phase separation-disruptive Y>A mutant intermolecular binding is detected for the C-terminal third of the molecule only (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A based on MD simulations.

claim: The dynamic modes identified in the intramolecular context are clearly different for all modeled proteins.
source: Interestingly, the dynamic modes identified in the intramolecular context are clearly different for all modeled proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A based on MD simulations.

claim: Intra- and intermolecular interactions rely on a similar pool of contacts by amino-acid type, but differ significantly if one analyzes specific sequence location of the interacting residues involved.
source: Specifically, intra- and intermolecular interactions rely on a similar pool of contacts by amino-acid type, but differ significantly if one analyzes specific sequence location of the interacting residues involved (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B based on MD simulations.

claim: There is a high correlation between the frequencies of different contacts by amino acid type when comparing intramolecular contacts in single-chain simulations and intermolecular contacts in multi-chain simulations.
source: For example, one observes a high correlation between the frequencies of different contacts by amino acid type when comparing intramolecular contacts in single-chain simulations and intermolecular contacts in multi-chain simulations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B based on MD simulations.

claim: This correlation is completely lost if one analyzes position-resolved statistics (2D pairwise contacts maps) or statistically defined interaction modes.
source: This correlation is completely lost if one analyzes position-resolved statistics (2D pairwise contacts maps) or statistically defined interaction modes (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in figures based on MD simulations.

claim: Proteins maintain core self-contacts and establish new ones with neighbors, but do not lose self-identity as expected in a polymer melt.
source: The latter suggests that proteins maintain core self-contacts and establish new ones with neighbors, but do not lose self-identity as expected in a polymer melt.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation analysis of interaction modes in the Results section.

claim: The observed 'symmetry breaking' between intra- and intermolecular mode of IDRs interactions is in line with the recent study by Bremer et al., 2022, and Martin et al., 2020.
source: The observed 'symmetry breaking' between intra- and intermolecular mode of IDRs interactions is in line with the recent study by Bremer et al., 2022, and (Martin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to prior work.

claim: Lge1-80 exhibits a relatively high net charge per residue (0.075).
source: In particular, Lge1-80 exhibits a relatively high net charge per residue (0.075), a non-uniform patterning of tyrosines (Ωaro = 0.47, p = 0.57, see Martin et al. for methodological details), and a high abundance of arginines
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence analysis.

claim: At the level of single molecules, extensive interactions involving R and Y residues result in a substantial compaction of the WT chain with the average radius of gyration <RgMD> = 1.58 ± 0.12 nm.
source: At the level of single molecules, extensive interactions involving R and Y residues result in a substantial compaction of the WT chain with the avaerage radius of gyration <RgMD> = 1.58 ± 0.12 nm (Figure 4A, see also Supplementary file 1 for details).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A based on MD simulations.

claim: The RgMD distributions of the R>K and Y>A variants cover a wider range and display significantly higher average values (1.81 ± 0.35 and 1.71 ± 0.29 nm, respectively).
source: In contrast, the RgMD distributions of the R>K and Y>A variants cover a wider range and display significantly higher average values (1.81 ± 0.35 and 1.71 ± 0.29 nm, respectively, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A based on MD simulations.

claim: All three Lge11-80 variants are more compact than predictions for a random coil of the same length (<Rgrc> = 2.50 nm).
source: This is in all three cases more compact as compared with the predictions for a random coil of the same length (<Rgrc> = 2.50 nm, Bernadó and Blackledge, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing MD results to theoretical predictions.

claim: In the crowded environment, WT adopts a compact organization with an almost invariant <RgMD> = 1.60 ± 0.22 nm when averaged over all 24 copies.
source: In the crowded environment, WT again adopts a compact organization with an almost invariant <RgMD> = 1.60 ± 0.22 nm when averaged over all 24 copies (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B based on MD simulations.

claim: The weakly self-interacting Y>A mutant unwinds toward more extended conformations in the crowded environment (<RgMD> = 1.97 ± 0.43 nm).
source: In the crowded environment, WT again adopts a compact organization with an almost invariant <RgMD> = 1.60 ± 0.22 nm when averaged over all 24 copies (Figure 4B), while the weakly self-interacting Y>A mutant unwinds toward more extended conformations (<RgMD> = 1.97 ± 0.43 nm).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B based on MD simulations.

claim: R>K comes closer to WT values in the crowded environment (<RgMD> = 1.67 ± 0.27 nm).
source: At the same time, R>K, being most loosely packed in the single-molecule context, comes closer to WT values in the crowded environment (<RgMD> = 1.67 ± 0.27 nm, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B based on MD simulations.

claim: The conformational behavior of IDPs in the bulk or in the crowded phase displays a clear sequence-specific character and cannot easily be generalized.
source: These results highlight the fact that the conformational behavior of IDPs in the bulk or in the crowded phase displays a clear sequence-specific character and cannot easily be generalized.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the MD simulation results in the Results section.

claim: Single-molecule translational diffusion coefficients of Lge11-80 variants are ~120 µm2/s for all three single-chain simulations.
source: Single-molecule translational diffusion coefficients of Lge11-80 variants obtained from fitting of MSD curves with an applied finite-size PBC correction and solvent viscosity rescaling (see Methods for details) are ~120 µm2/s for all three single-chain simulations or anywhere between 100 and 150 µm2/s for multi-chain simulations and different Lge11-80 variants (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C based on MD simulations.

claim: The diffusion constant of ubiquitin (Rg = 1.32 nm, 76 aa, 8.6 kDa) at the protein concentration of 8.6 mg/ml is 149 µs2/s.
source: In comparison, the diffusion constant of the similarly sized ubiquitin (Rg = 1.32 nm, 76 aa, 8.6 kDa) at the protein concentration of 8.6 mg/ml is 149 µs2/s (Altieri et al., 1995)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to prior work for comparison.

claim: The diffusion constant of GFP (Rg = 2.8 nm, 238 aa, 27 kDa) at the concentration of 0.5–3 mg/ml is ~90 µs2/s.
source: while that of GFP (Rg = 2.8 nm, 238 aa, 27 kDa) at the concentration of 0.5–3 mg/ml is ~90 µs2/s (Baum et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to prior work for comparison.

claim: The diffusional dynamics captured by the simulations may be realistic.
source: This suggests that the diffusional dynamics captured by our simulations may be realistic.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with experimental values for other proteins.

claim: The viscosity values in single-chain simulations of the three Lge11-80 variants are all similar to each other and are close to the calculated solvent viscosity for TIP4P-D water/0.1 M NaCl of 0.83 mPa*s.
source: The obtained viscosity values (see Methods for details) in single-chain simulations of the three Lge11-80 variants (effective concentration of 2.3 mg/ml) are all similar to each other and are close to the calculated solvent viscosity for TIP4P-D water/0.1 M NaCl of 0.83 mPa*s (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F based on MD simulations.

claim: In the crowded multi-chain systems, the viscosity systematically increases by about 20%.
source: In the crowded multi-chain systems (effective concentration of 6–7 mg/ml), the viscosity systematically increases by about 20% and is again similar for all three Lge11-80 variants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F based on MD simulations.

claim: In both single- and multi-chain simulations, the WT translational diffusion coefficients are somewhat lower than for either mutant.
source: In both single- and multi-chain simulations, the WT translational diffusion coefficients are somewhat lower than for either mutant (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C based on MD simulations.

claim: The WT diffusion coefficient drops by approximately 20% over the last 0.3 µs of the trajectory.
source: For instance, the WT diffusion coefficient drops by approximately 20% over the last 0.3 µs of the trajectory (Figure 4C), which correlates with the formation of a single percolating cluster in the system (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C based on MD simulations.

claim: In the crowded multi-chain environment, there is a significant decrease in Sconf for all three variants, with the biggest change seen for WT and the smallest for Y>A.
source: Interestingly, in the crowded multi-chain environment, we observe a significant decrease in Sconf for all three variants, with the biggest change seen for WT and the smallest for Y>A (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D based on MD simulations.

claim: The crowding involves a conformational reorganization of the molecules toward decreasing the available free volume, that is increasing their compactness (volume fraction) φ.
source: These results suggest that the crowding involves a conformational reorganization of the molecules toward decreasing the available free volume, that is increasing their compactness (volume fraction) φ, defined here as the ratio between the van der Waals and the hydrodynamic volume of a molecule.
evidence: This is inferred from the entropy changes observed in MD simulations.

claim: There is a substantial increase in Sconf associated with the Y>A mutation of the WT in both single- and multi-chain contexts.
source: Finally, there is a substantial increase in Sconf associated with the Y>A mutation of the WT in both single- and multi-chain contexts, in contrast with the R>K mutation, where a much weaker effect is observed (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4E based on MD simulations.

claim: An increase in φ in the crowded environment correlates directly with an unfavorable ΔSconf (Pearson R is –0.6).
source: Importantly, an increase in φ in the crowded environment correlates directly with an unfavorable ΔSconf (Figure 4F, Pearson R is –0.6), an effect which can potentially be compensated for by the favorable enthalpy upon forming the extensive multivalent interaction network as observed for the WT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4F based on MD simulations.

claim: ΔSconf correlates poorly with the average number of bound partners (valency; Pearson R is –0.3).
source: Conversely, ΔSconf correlates poorly with the average number of bound partners (valency; Pearson R is –0.3) and there is no correlation between the compactness φ, and the valency of interactions (not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MD simulations.

claim: Compactness and valency are mutually largely independent and are the key parameters describing the organization of the crowded phase.
source: Being mutually largely independent, these two characteristics of protein molecules – compactness and valency – are the key parameters describing the organization of the corresponding crowded phase, which generally reflect the entropic and the enthalpic contributions to self-organization, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the MD simulation results in the Results section.

claim: The slope (A) and the intercept (B) of the linear regression for the log R vs log Mw plots are similar between the simulations and the model (2.33 vs 2.42 and 1.13 vs 1.11, respectively).
source: Moreover, the slope (A, Equation 10) and the intercept (B, Equation 11) of the linear regression for the log R vs log Mw plots are also similar between the simulations and the model (2.33 vs 2.42 and 1.13 vs 1.11, respectively) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B comparing MD simulations to the fractal model.

claim: Fractal organization is present even at the shortest scale, that is at the level of MD simulation boxes.
source: These non-trivial correspondences suggest that fractal organization is present even at the shortest scale, that is at the level of MD simulation boxes.
evidence: This is inferred from the agreement between MD simulations and the fractal model.

claim: In order to keep the ratio of size-to-concentration fixed, protein compactness must decrease non-linearly with increasing valency.
source: Generally, in order to keep the ratio of size-to-concentration fixed, protein compactness must decrease non-linearly with increasing valency (Figure 5B, dashed lines).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B based on the fractal model.

claim: Perturbation of compactness and valency due to the two types of studied mutations can result in a decrease of the apparent concentration in condensates of fixed size.
source: Accordingly, perturbation of compactness and valency due to the two types of studied mutations can result in a decrease of the apparent concentration in condensates of fixed size.
evidence: This is inferred from the fractal model in the Results section.

claim: The compactness of IDPs is not a stable parameter and is tunable by different factors (temperature, pH, ionic strength, etc.).
source: Importantly, the compactness of IDPs is not a stable parameter and is tunable by different factors (temperature, pH, ionic strength, etc.) (Uversky, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to prior work.

claim: IDP concentration inside condensates may be adaptable and tunable.
source: This, in turn, also suggests that IDP concentration inside condensates may also be adaptable and tunable.
evidence: This is inferred from the tunability of IDP compactness in the Results section.

claim: Unwinding or compaction of an IDP due to any factor would change the apparent concentration and density in the condensates.
source: Thus, unwinding or compaction of an IDP due to any factor would change the apparent concentration and density in the condensates.
evidence: This is inferred from the fractal model in the Results section.

claim: The fractal dimension df describes the topology of molecular clusters.
source: Thus, the slope of the line in the log R vs. log Mw plot (A) is equal to the fractal dimension df, which describes the topology of molecular clusters (Carpineti and Giglio, 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to prior work.

claim: The WT condensate exhibits a df of 2.42.
source: Specifically, while the WT condensate simulated here exhibits a df of 2.42 and is also experimentally found to undergo robust phase separation
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the fractal model applied to MD simulation data.

claim: The R>K mutant exhibits a df of 2.09.
source: the R>K mutant exhibits a lower df of 2.09 and undergoes phase separation under a more limited set of conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the fractal model applied to MD simulation data.

claim: df is 1.63 for the Y>A mutant.
source: Even more extremely, df is 1.63 for the Y>A mutant (Figure 5C), which does not undergo phase separation and can be thought of as an object between 1D and 2D.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C based on the fractal model applied to MD simulation data.

claim: The modeled WT Lge11-80 condensate exhibits a densely packed fractal geometry.
source: In agreement with its micrometer-scale behavior observed in vitro, the modeled WT Lge11-80 condensate exhibits a densely packed fractal geometry.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the reconstructed condensate models.

claim: The reconstructed Y>A cluster exhibits an elongated, filamentous topology of low dimensionality.
source: In contrast, the reconstructed Y>A cluster exhibits an elongated, filamentous topology of low dimensionality (Figure 6B), which may preclude the formation of well-defined phase-separated droplets (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B based on the reconstructed condensate models.

claim: The R>K cluster exhibits an intermediate topology.
source: The R>K cluster exhibits an intermediate topology.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the reconstructed condensate models.

claim: The Y>A cluster occupies a significantly larger volume as compared to the R>K cluster and especially the WT.
source: The clusters shown in Figure 6B were generated using 1024 primary particles in all three cases: clearly, the Y>A cluster occupies a significantly larger volume as compared to the R>K cluster and especially the WT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B based on the reconstructed condensate models.

claim: The three reconstructed systems exhibit holes and cavities of different sizes.
source: In particular, the three reconstructed systems exhibit holes and cavities of different sizes (see Videos 4–6 to zoom in the internal organization of the model condensates), with Y>A being most extreme in this regard.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Videos 4–6 based on the reconstructed condensate models.

claim: Mutations of R and Y residues induce perturbations at the level of both intra- and intermolecular interaction networks.
source: We have shown that mutations of R and Y residues induce perturbations at the level of both intra- and intermolecular interaction networks, and result in conformational effects that can be related to the phase behavior and the ability to form condensates as detected by light microscopy.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: The characteristic descriptors of protein behavior in the crowded phase, valency, and compactness (volume fraction) are sufficient to describe the structural organization of condensates across length scales.
source: Specifically, the characteristic descriptors of protein behavior in the crowded phase, valency, and compactness (volume fraction) are shown to be sufficient to describe the structural organization of condensates across length scales in the context of the proposed analytical fractal model.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: The studied mutations substantially change either just the valency (R>K) or both the valency and compactness (Y>A) of Lge11-80 polypeptides.
source: Importantly, the studied mutations substantially change either just the valency (R>K) or both the valency and compactness (Y>A) of Lge11-80 polypeptides as shown in MD simulations.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section based on MD simulations.

claim: The values of valency and compactness obtained from simulations are consistent with the difference in FRAP recovery dynamics observed for WT and R>K.
source: As a further indication of its general quality, the values of valency and compactness obtained from simulations are consistent with the difference in FRAP recovery dynamics observed for WT and R>K.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section comparing simulations to experiments.

claim: The recovery in centrally bleached condensates is faster for WT than for the R>K mutant, which can be related to the higher compactness of WT particle across scales.
source: Thus, the recovery in centrally bleached condensates is faster for WT than for the R>K mutant, which can be related to the higher compactness of WT particle across scales, as compared to R>K (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section comparing FRAP results to simulation-derived compactness.

claim: The FRAP results for the condensates bleached in the peripheral area highlight the contribution of valency to condensate formation.
source: On the other hand, the FRAP results for the condensates bleached in the peripheral area highlight the contribution of valency to condensate formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting FRAP results.

claim: The recovery is about three times faster for the R>K mutant, which could potentially be related to the lower valency of interactions.
source: Indeed, the recovery is about three times faster for the R>K mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), which could potentially be related to the lower valency of interactions and the ease of replacement of inactivated fluorescent species or/and exchange with proteins in the bulk.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting FRAP results.

claim: In the fractal model, the changes in protein valency and compactness translate to different scaling behavior and, subsequently, different topology of the condensates.
source: In the fractal model, the changes in protein valency and compactness translate to different scaling behavior and, subsequently, different topology of the condensates.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the fractal model.

claim: The proposed model predicts the existence and provides a quantitative characterization of topological properties of pre-percolation finite-size clusters.
source: Importantly, the proposed model predicts the existence and provides a quantitative characterization of topological properties of pre-percolation finite-size clusters that are in line with the recent findings (Kar et al., 2022; Mittag and Pappu, 2022; Pappu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to prior work.

claim: The model provides the fractal dimension (df) of protein clusters and enables evaluation of different scale-dependent properties of clusters of arbitrary size.
source: More generally, the model provides the fractal dimension (df) of protein clusters and enables evaluation of different scale-dependent properties of clusters of arbitrary size, including protein density as a function of cluster size (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the fractal model.

claim: MD simulations of proteins in the crowded context on the length scale of tens of nanometers can be used in combination with cluster-cluster aggregation algorithms to derive atomistically resolved models of the 3D organization of fractal clusters of any chosen size.
source: Finally, MD simulations of proteins in the crowded context on the length scale of tens of nanometers can be used in combination with cluster-cluster aggregation algorithms to derive atomistically resolved models of the 3D organization of fractal clusters of any chosen size (Figure 6A and B, and Videos 4–6).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the methodology.

claim: Fractal behavior is naturally related to percolation phenomena.
source: Importantly, fractal behavior, as explored in the present work, is naturally related to percolation phenomena.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on general knowledge.

claim: Direct links between the fractal dimension defining scaling principles in self-similar clusters and critical exponents in different percolation models have been provided.
source: For instance, direct links between the fractal dimension defining scaling principles in self-similar clusters and critical exponents in different percolation models have been provided (Kapitulnik et al., 1984; Stauffer et al., 1982).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to prior work.

claim: Concentrations at which network transition is expected should be lower for WT than for either mutant.
source: This perspective suggests that concentrations at which network transition is expected should be lower for WT than for either mutant, as indeed observed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the analysis and experimental observations.

claim: The ability of IDRs to form low-dimensional fractal structures (df is in a range of 1.6–1.9) upon the disruption of their tendency to phase separate by a polyalanine insertion was demonstrated experimentally for synthetic elastin-like polypeptides.
source: Of note, the ability of IDRs to form low-dimensional fractal structures (df is in a range of 1.6–1.9) upon the disruption of their tendency to phase separate by a polyalanine insertion was demonstrated experimentally for synthetic elastin-like polypeptides (Roberts et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to prior work.

claim: Fractal systems are characterized by a remarkable property that their packing density is a function of the length scale on which it is examined.
source: Namely, fractal systems are characterized by a remarkable property that their packing density is a function of the length scale on which it is examined (Stanley, 1984).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to prior work.

claim: Fractal organization enables high local concentration of biomolecules at short length scales and, simultaneously, low global concentration at long length scales.
source: Translated to the question of biomolecular condensates, fractal organization enables high local concentration of biomolecules at short length scales and, simultaneously, low global concentration at long length scales, as illustrated in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the fractal model.

claim: Fractal systems are characterized by the existence of holes, that is unoccupied regions of space, whose size covers a wide range of length scales.
source: Importantly, fractal systems are characterized by the existence of holes, that is unoccupied regions of space, whose size covers a wide range of length scales (Stanley, 1984).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to prior work.

claim: The µm-sized WT Lge11-80 droplets are fully permeable to dextrans in vitro, even up to Mw = 2000 kDa or Rg ~27 nm.
source: The observation that the µm-sized WT Lge11-80 droplets are fully permeable to dextrans in vitro (Gallego et al., 2020), even up to Mw = 2000 kDa or Rg ~27 nm (Armstrong et al., 2004; Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to prior work and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The organization of WT Lge11-80 droplets allows for large holes (~55 nm in diameter or more).
source: suggests that their organization allows for large holes (~55 nm in diameter or more).
evidence: This is inferred from the permeability data in the Discussion section.

claim: The dimensionality of WT condensates is below 3 (df = 2.42).
source: This is consistent with our fractal model, which proposes that the dimensionality of WT condensates is below 3 (df = 2.42, Figure 6, Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the fractal model.

claim: The multiscale nature of biomolecular condensates points to the possible formation of clusters with sizes well below the resolution limit of light microscopy.
source: Finally, the multiscale nature of biomolecular condensates, as embodied in the statistical fractal model, also points to the possible formation of clusters with sizes well below the resolution limit of light microscopy.
evidence: This is inferred from the fractal model in the Discussion section.

claim: In vitro Lge1 assembles a liquid-like core that is surrounded by an enzymatic outer shell formed by the E3 ubiquitin ligase Bre1.
source: In particular, it was shown that in vitro Lge1 assembles a liquid-like core that is surrounded by an enzymatic outer shell formed by the E3 ubiquitin ligase Bre1 (Gallego et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to prior work.

claim: The fractal model predicts the coexistence of differently sized clusters within a condensate.
source: Finally, the fractal model predicts the coexistence of differently sized clusters within a condensate, as reported recently (Kar et al., 2022), which have a characteristic scaling of mass with condensate size in the nm to µm range.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to prior work.

claim: A linearly decreasing intensity as a function of the scattering vector in a log-log representation is expected by the fractal model.
source: This prediction of the model can be tested using static light scattering (SLS) techniques and will be a subject of our future work: a linearly decreasing intensity as a function of the scattering vector in a log-log representation, as frequently seen for different colloidal systems, is expected by the fractal model (Lazzari et al., 2016; Lin et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to prior work.

claim: Fractal dimension can be estimated from SLS experiments as the limiting value of scattering curves for high values of the product of the scattering vector q and the average cluster size <Rg>.
source: In fact, fractal dimension can be estimated from SLS experiments as the limiting value of scattering curves for high values of the product of the scattering vector q and the average cluster size <Rg> (Hagiwara et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to prior work.

claim: In diffusion-limited cluster aggregation (DLCA), the rate of cluster formation is determined by the time it takes for colloidal particles to encounter each other and every encounter leads to binding.
source: In diffusion-limited cluster aggregation (DLCA), the rate of cluster formation is determined by the time it takes for colloidal particles to encounter each other and every encounter leads to binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on general knowledge of colloid chemistry.

claim: In reaction-limited cluster aggregation (RLCA), particles need to overcome a repulsive barrier before binding and not every encounter is productive.
source: In reaction-limited cluster aggregation (RLCA), particles need to overcome a repulsive barrier before binding and not every encounter is productive.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on general knowledge of colloid chemistry.

claim: Both DLCA and RLCA regimes result in fractal behavior.
source: Both regimes result in fractal behavior, with DLCA leading to looser structural organization and lower fractal dimensions and RLCA leading to more compact structural organization and higher fractal dimensions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on general knowledge of colloid chemistry.

claim: df is ~1.8 for DLCA and ~2.1 for RLCA.
source: Computer simulations and scattering experiments show that df is ~1.8 for DLCA and ~2.1 for RLCA (Lazzari et al., 2016; Lin et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to prior work.

claim: The two regimes of colloid cluster formation are universal and do not depend on the chemical nature of the underlying particles.
source: Importantly, Meakin and colleagues have shown that the two regimes of colloid cluster formation are universal and do not depend on the chemical nature of the underlying particles, making them an attractive paradigm for modeling the multiscale structure of biomolecular condensates as applied here (Lin et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to prior work.

claim: Recent studies have demonstrated the possibility to tune condensate properties in vitro and in vivo by manipulating the aromatic residue content and molecular weight in IDPs.
source: Indeed, recent studies have demonstrated the possibility to tune condensate properties in vitro and in vivo by manipulating the aromatic residue content and molecular weight in IDPs (Dzuricky et al., 2020) or the size of disordered linkers and valency in modular proteins (Lasker et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to prior work.
